questions.q: Why can't a sale credited to multiple salespeople be modeled with a simple one-to-many relationship?
options: The real-world relationship is genuinely many-to-many — one sale can have several salespeople, and one salesperson can be credited on many sales
SQL Server does not support one-to-many relationships in dimensional models
Fact tables are not allowed to reference dimension tables directly
Salespeople cannot be represented as a dimension
questions.explain: Some real-world relationships are genuinely many-to-many on both sides, and no fact table design trick converts that into a true one-to-many relationship.

options: A third table storing one row per valid combination, resolving a many-to-many relationship into two one-to-many relationships
A dimension table that stores historical versions of a changing attribute
A fact table that stores only numeric measures with no keys
A staging table used only during the ETL load window
questions.explain: Instead of one direct many-to-many relationship, the fact relates to the bridge table, and the bridge table relates to the dimension — two clean one-to-many relationships.

questions.q: In Microsoft's Fabric Warehouse example, how does the Customer dimension relate to the Transaction fact table?
options: Only through a Customer Account bridge table, because customers can have multiple accounts and accounts can have multiple customers
Directly, with a simple one-to-many foreign key, just like the Account dimension
Customer is not related to Transaction at all in this model
Customer and Transaction are merged into a single table
questions.explain: The Account dimension relates to the fact table directly, but Customer relates to it only via the bridge table, since the customer-account relationship is many-to-many.

questions.q: Why is a bridge table containing only identifier columns considered a factless fact table?
options: A row records that an association occurred, with no measures to sum — only a count of rows is meaningful
It is a mistake in dimensional modeling and should always be avoided
Factless fact tables are a completely different, unrelated concept
Because bridge tables never contain any keys at all
questions.explain: A factless fact table has no numeric measures — its rows simply record that something happened (or that an association exists), which matches a bridge table with only foreign key columns.

questions.q: If a single sale is split three ways among salespeople A, B, and C, how many rows would that sale produce in a Sale Salesperson bridge table?
options: Three rows — one per sale-salesperson pairing, all pointing at the same sale
One row, with all three salespeople listed in a single column
Zero rows, because bridge tables don't store sales with multiple salespeople
Nine rows, as the Cartesian product of all salespeople in the company
questions.explain: A bridge table stores one row per valid combination, so a three-way split sale produces exactly three bridge rows, each pointing at the same sale and a different salesperson.
